--- title: "Supervised Learning: Linear Discriminant Analysis and Factor Analysis" author: "
SURE 2026

Department of Statistics & Data Science
Carnegie Mellon University" footer: "[36-SURE.github.io/2026](https://36-sure.github.io/2026)" format: revealjs: theme: theme.scss chalkboard: true smaller: true slide-number: c/t code-line-numbers: false linestretch: 1.25 html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" --- ## Principal Components Analysis (PCA) Recap - **Unsupervised** method of dimensionality reduction that aims to find the directions of maximum variance in a dataset - End goal is to have a smaller set of variables (principal components) that capture the most important patterns in the data. These principal components - are linear combinations of the features - are mutally uncorrelated - Keep the principal components that explain a certain percentage of the total variance in the data # Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) ## Overview of LDA - Aims to find the linear combination of features that best separates the classes in a dataset - This makes LDA a **supervised learning method** for dimensionality reduction - End goal is to reduce the dimensionality of the data while preserving the information that is most relevant for class discrimination ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1400/1*ELmUt0gXZPm3s5bfcr5KOg.png){fig-align='center' width=20%} ::: ::: ## LDA visually Let's say we are interested in deciding whether to give someone a medication based on two features $x$ and $y$. - Blue: responders to the medication - Red: non-responders to the medication ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](15-lda-fa_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## LDA visually ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} - For a **two-class** problem, LDA finds a single projection direction that maximizes the separation between classes relative to the variation within classes. - The original data are projected onto this axis, reducing the problem from $p$ dimensions (where $p$ = number of predictors, here $p=2$) to one dimension. - What's the best way to determine the projection direction? - One option (bad) is to ignore $y$ and project the data down onto the $x$ axis. ::: ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](15-lda-fa_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## LDA visually - LDA finds the projection direction that produces the greatest separation between responders and non-responders - This is perpendicular to the boundary that we might draw if we were separating these points by hand (dashed line on left plot) ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](15-lda-fa_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=384} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](15-lda-fa_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=384} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## LDA visually We can now see the data projected onto the new axis in a way that maximizes the separation between responders and non-responders! ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](15-lda-fa_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## What does the "best" projection mean? A good projection should... - maximize the distance between class means - minimize the variation (sometimes called scatter) within each class Therefore, for two classes, the *best* axis is chosen to maximize the ratio $\frac{(\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2}{s_1^2 + s_2^2}$, where $\mu_x$ represents the mean of class $x$ and $s_x^2$ the scatter ## Assumptions of LDA ## Adding more dimensions What happens if we have more than two predictors? ## Data: Shohei Ohtani pitches Pitches by Shohei Ohtani over the last month (May 20, 2026-June 20, 2026) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ohtani <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/36-SURE/2026/main/data/ohtani.csv") theme_set(theme_light()) ``` ::: ## EDA on Ohtani's pitch tendencies How often does Ohtani throw each pitch, and how do their speeds vary? ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ohtani |> count(pitch_type) |> mutate(prop = n/sum(n)) |> ggplot(aes(x=fct_reorder(pitch_type, -prop), y = prop))+ geom_col()+ labs(x = "Pitch type")+ theme_light(base_size = 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](15-lda-fa_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ohtani |> ggplot(aes(x=release_speed, y=pitch_type, color=pitch_type))+ geom_boxplot()+ labs(x="Release speed (mph)", y="")+ theme_light(base_size = 20)+ theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](15-lda-fa_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Step 1: Preparing the data First, determine class and variables of interest. Our research question will be: *can we discern Shohei Ohtani's pitch types from his release speed and position?* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ohtani_subset <- ohtani |> dplyr::select(pitch_type, release_speed, release_pos_x, release_pos_y, release_pos_z) ``` ::: Next, create training and test data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #install.packages("rsample") library(rsample) set.seed(623) data_split <- initial_split(ohtani_subset, prop = 0.6, strata = pitch_type) train <- training(data_split) test <- testing(data_split) ``` ::: ## Step 2: Fitting the LDA What does each part of the output tell us? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(MASS) lda_mod <- lda(pitch_type~., train) lda_mod ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lda(pitch_type ~ ., data = train) Prior probabilities of groups: CU FF FS SI SL ST 0.082142857 0.485714286 0.060714286 0.042857143 0.003571429 0.325000000 Group means: release_speed release_pos_x release_pos_y release_pos_z CU 76.27826 -1.696087 54.13348 6.220435 FF 97.91103 -2.105956 53.82022 5.554632 FS 89.88235 -2.137647 53.78824 5.619412 SI 95.51667 -1.994167 53.78667 5.538333 SL 88.00000 -1.960000 54.11000 6.010000 ST 84.64945 -2.176374 53.92374 5.537473 Coefficients of linear discriminants: LD1 LD2 LD3 LD4 release_speed 0.5518899 -0.1090227 0.01667026 0.05765398 release_pos_x 1.6600838 -1.9191138 7.37820567 -3.69240184 release_pos_y 0.5096036 1.3009621 6.59849863 4.91813293 release_pos_z -0.7423821 -8.0776372 -6.97652798 1.74542281 Proportion of trace: LD1 LD2 LD3 LD4 0.8870 0.1066 0.0046 0.0018 ``` ::: ::: ## Step 3: Making predictions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_preds <- predict(lda_mod, test)$class #mean(test_preds == test$pitch_type) table(Predicted = test_preds, Actual = test$pitch_type) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Actual Predicted CU FF FS SI SL ST CU 21 0 0 0 0 0 FF 0 88 0 1 0 0 FS 0 1 6 0 1 1 SI 0 0 1 1 0 0 SL 0 0 0 0 3 0 ST 0 0 1 0 0 64 ``` ::: ::: ## Step 4: What features contribute? - We *didn't* standardize the variables beforehand, so we cannot use the size of the coefficients to understand which variables drive each axis - If we had standardized beforehand, we might could interpret like "A one sd increase in release speed changes the LD1 score by about X units, whereas a one sd change release height changes LD1 by only about Y units". - However, we can calculate the correlation of the LD scores with each variable. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- predict(lda_mod)$x cor(train |> dplyr::select(-pitch_type), scores) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` LD1 LD2 LD3 LD4 release_speed 0.9985802 0.02755992 -0.03958774 0.02260379 release_pos_x -0.2302403 -0.76187799 0.42450838 -0.43165262 release_pos_y -0.4879135 -0.24316385 0.37423851 0.75017149 release_pos_z -0.4834677 -0.85837824 -0.01957474 0.17047771 ``` ::: ::: ## Other uses of LDA ## Similarities between PCA and LDA - Both methods are dimensionality reduction techniques - Both methods rank the new axes in order of importance - PC1 (first new axis that PCA creates) accounts for most variation in the data - LD1 (first new axis that LDA creates) accounts for most variation between categories - Both methods let you see which variables are driving the new axes - PCA: look at the loading scores - LDA: which variables correlate with the new axes ## Connecting to other concepts **Clustering** . . . **Logistic regression**

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
